I have now gathered material from multiple sources. Here are my verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Ezekiel 44 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1–2: The Shut East Gate

**Traditional Reading:**

The prophet is led back from the altar area to the eastern gate of the outer court (or inner court — commentators differ) and finds it shut. The Lord explains that it must remain permanently closed because "the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered by it." This refers to the return of the divine glory in Ezekiel 43:1–5. The shut gate is a sign that God will never again depart from His temple (cf. Ezek 37:24–28). It is "not a menacing symbol but an encouraging one" — a seal of God's permanent dwelling. As a mark of respect to an Eastern monarch, the gate by which the king entered was thereafter shut to all others (Job 12:14; Isa 22:22; Rev 3:7).

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The gate is "separated for God's use alone." Even priests may not enter this way. "Once Yahweh has made his grand entrance into his temple … no one else may enter here" (Block, cited). The current sealed Golden Gate in Jerusalem is *not* the fulfillment — the dimensions differ. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **JFB**: "Shut to the people … but open to 'the prince' (v. 3), he holding the place of God in political concerns, as the priests do in spiritual." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/44.htm)
- **Gill**: Sees the shut gate as a picture of the Gospel church in the latter day — a "garden enclosed, a spring shut up," into which "no natural or unregenerate man should enter" (Isa 52:1; Rev 21:27). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/44.htm)
- **Benson (Methodist)**: The order was given "both to perpetuate the remembrance of the solemn entrance of the glory of the Lord … and also to possess the minds of the people with a deep reverence for the Divine Majesty." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Constable (Evangelical/Baptist)**: "Its sealed condition guaranteed God’s promise that He would never depart from the temple again." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)

**Catholic/Patristic Reading:**

Clarke (cited in Guzik) notes that this verse has been used by Roman Catholics "to prove the perpetual virginity of the mother of our Lord." Gill observes that "some of the ancients have interpreted it of the Virgin Mary, by whom Christ came into this world … a virgin, who had never known man, and as is thought never did after the birth of Christ." He adds that this is approved "not only by Papists, but by many Protestant writers." The east gate through which only God entered and which remains forever shut is read typologically: as Christ alone passed through Mary's womb without opening it, so the gate remains shut to all others.

- (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/) — see Clarke citation
- (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/44.htm)

---

### v. 3: The Prince

**Traditional Reading — Major Disagreement Among Traditions:**

The "prince" (Hebrew *nasi*) is permitted to sit in the gate complex (its vestibule/porch) and "eat bread before the LORD." He enters and exits by the same gate. Who is this prince?

**View 1 — Not the Messiah, but a future Davidic civil ruler (majority of older Protestant commentators):**

- **JFB (Reformed)**: "The prince must mean the civil ruler under Messiah. … He cannot be King Messiah, as He never would offer a burnt offering for Himself, as the prince is to do (Ezek 46:4)." The prince "represents Messiah" and stands "in a place of peculiar nearness to God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/44.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik, Charismatic)**: The prince "is likely David, whose future rule over Israel is mentioned several times in Ezekiel (34:23–25, 37:25)." The fact that the prince must offer a sin offering (45:22) and has sons (46:16) "means it is unlikely that the prince is Jesus Messiah." He is "Messiah's representative in a special sense." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **Constable (Evangelical/Baptist)**: The prince "is not Messiah" for the same reasons — sin offering, natural children, not a priest. "The exact identity … is presently unknown, but he will apparently function as Messiah’s administrative representative." Some suggest resurrected David. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Gray's Concise Commentary**: "This cannot mean the Messiah, because the prince requires a sin-offering. … Doubtless this prince is a future prince of the house of David." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/ezekiel-44.html)

**View 2 — The Prince is the Messiah (older Jewish interpreters, some Reformed):**

- **Gill (Baptist, older)**: "The King Messiah, as Kimchi and Ben Melech rightly interpret it, is here meant … he who is the Prince of peace; Michael the great Prince; the Prince of life." Gill spiritualises the eating of bread as Christ sitting at His table with His saints "in his word and ordinances before the Lord." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/44.htm)
- **Ellicott (Anglican)**: "The Rabbis understood this to refer to the Messiah, and unquestionably the same person must be meant as by David in Ezek 34:23–24; 37:24. This gives another and a conclusive reason for regarding the sacrificial worship of Ezekiel 46 as symbolical." The prince is not endued with priestly functions — he partakes of sacrificial meals but does not officiate. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/44.htm)
- **Ligonier (Reformed)**: "Jesus fulfills Ezekiel's vision of the prince. He is identified with both Yahweh and His people, being truly God and truly man (John 1:1–18). And He offered the only sacrifice needed for us to come regularly before God — the once-for-all sacrifice of Himself (Heb 9:11–28)." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/sacrifices-prince)
- **Bible.org notes**: "This is a Messianic reference (cf. 34:24; 37:24–25)." The phrase "eat bread before the Lord" is "a metaphor of worship and covenant (cf. Gen 31:54; Exod 24:9–11)." (https://bible.org/book/export/html/21739)

**View 3 — The prince is a post-exilic civil governor (Benson, Methodist):**

- **Benson**: "By the prince here is probably meant the chief governor of the Jews after the captivity, such as were Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, for Sheshbazzar, or Zerubbabel, is called the prince of Judah, Ezra 1:8." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-44.html)

---

### v. 4–5: The Glory of the LORD Fills the Temple; "Mark Well"

**Traditional Reading:**

Since the east gate is shut, the guide brings Ezekiel by the north gate to the front of the temple. He again sees the glory of the LORD filling the temple and falls on his face. The Lord commands him to pay the closest attention ("mark well … see with your eyes and hear with your ears") to all the statutes concerning the temple — especially "the entrance … along with all the exits of the sanctuary," because the critical issue is who may enter and who must be excluded.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "The glory Ezekiel saw fill the temple in Ezekiel 43:1–4 remained there. As promised, it would be His dwelling place forever." The command to "mark well who may enter" sets up the distinction relevant even to the eternal state (Rev 21:7–8; 22:14–15). The absence of any mention of the high priest or the holy of holies is "remarkable" (Block). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **Constable**: "The new reference to the glory of God simply makes clear that it is the return of God to the temple that serves as a basis for the regulations to follow." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Gill**: Interprets the north gate as having "some respect to the churches in these our northern parts of the world, in their now declining circumstances." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/44.htm)
- **Ellicott**: Notes that Ezekiel is "carried to the north gate" described as "before the house." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/44.htm)

---

### v. 6–9: Rebuke to Israel; Exclusion of Foreigners

**Traditional Reading:**

God addresses "the rebellious house of Israel" and declares He has had enough of their abominations. The specific sin was bringing "foreigners uncircumcised in both heart and flesh" into the sanctuary, thereby defiling it and breaking the covenant. In the past, Israel failed to guard the holy things, even appointing foreigners to keep charge of the sanctuary. The decree: "No foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh may enter My sanctuary."

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "In the last days of Solomon's Temple the priests had allowed anyone, even uncovenanted pagans, to act as priests and temple servants" (Wright, cited). The ancient Near East commonly used foreign captives as temple servants. In the future temple, "there would be a true separation and those not in covenant could not even enter His sanctuary." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **Ellicott**: Notes that the Law actually allowed foreigners to offer sacrifices (Lev 17:10–12; Num 15:14–29; 1 Kgs 8:41–43). The censure is for admitting those "uncircumcised in heart as well as in flesh, i.e., ungodly men who had no real purpose to worship God." The prohibition in v. 9 is not against all uncircumcised persons (since foreign residents are provided for in Ezek 47:22–23) — the emphasis is on the *uncircumcised in heart*. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/44.htm)
- **Gill**: Applies this spiritually: "unregenerate men may not be admitted members of a Gospel church … and much less should such be admitted to public service, to preach the word, and administer ordinances." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/44.htm)
- **Constable**: "Believing foreigners could offer sacrifices there and assist the priests, but they could not serve as priests." In the millennial temple, "foreigners (uncircumcised in heart and flesh, i.e., unbelieving Gentiles) would not be allowed to enter the temple proper." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)

---

### v. 10–14: The Degraded Levites

**Traditional Reading:**

The Levites who "wandered away from Me when Israel went astray … after their idols" will bear their iniquity. Yet they are not utterly cast off — they will still minister in the sanctuary as gatekeepers, slaughtering the burnt offerings and serving the people. But they are barred from approaching God as priests, from the holy things, and from the Most Holy Place. They will "bear the shame of the abominations they have committed." This is both mercy and discipline — they are restored to *some* service, but demoted from the higher priestly functions.

- **Peake's (Modern Critical)**: This is one of "the most important" passages in Ezekiel and "has played a great part in the critical rearrangement of OT literature." Under the old system, "priests and Levites were synonymous and every Levite might be a priest." Ezekiel "distinguishes sharply between them," and this distinction "is presupposed throughout the priestly literature in the middle of the Pentateuch." The Levites' degradation is "a penalty for their participation in the idolatrous worship of the high places." Before Josiah's reform, Deuteronomy 18:6–8 permitted country priests to officiate in Jerusalem on equal terms, but the Jerusalem priests thwarted this (2 Kgs 23:9). Ezekiel solves the problem by admitting the country Levites "to the sanctuary service, but only to the humbler offices." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Far from causing the Levites to gloat with pride over their assignment, this act of divine grace will precipitate a sense of shame and intense unworthiness" (Block, cited). The fact of discipline during this temple period demonstrates "this does not belong to the eternal realm, but to the millennial period." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **Constable**: "Most of the Levitical priests, who had been responsible for profaning the temple in the past, would have to bear the punishment for their iniquity." They would do what foreigners previously did — overseeing gates, serving in the precincts, slaughtering animals. Under Mosaic law the offerer killed the victim, not the priest — this represents a change. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Benson (Methodist)**: Refers to 2 Kings 23:9 — Josiah discharged idolatrous priests from altar service. Many priests and Levites from the first temple lived to see the second (Ezra 3:12). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **JFB**: "Like people, like priest" (Jer 5:31; Hos 4:9) — the sins of priesthood and people reacted on one another. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/44.htm)

---

### v. 15–16: The Sons of Zadok

**Traditional Reading:**

In contrast, "the Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok, who kept charge of My sanctuary when the Israelites went astray," receive the privilege of approaching God, ministering before Him, offering "the fat and the blood," entering the sanctuary, and drawing near to His table. Zadok was the priest who remained faithful to David during Absalom's rebellion and anointed Solomon king (1 Kgs 1–2). The name becomes emblematic of all faithful priests.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "With great emphasis, God declared that the ministry of the priests was fundamentally to God Himself" — note the repeated "to Me." "Every believer is a priest unto God … believers in general (and God's servants in particular) have their first service to God Himself." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **Ellicott**: "As Zadok had continued faithful in the rebellion of Adonijah, when even the high priest and life-long friend of David went astray (1 Kgs 1:7–8), so all the faithful priests in the time of apostasy were called 'sons of Zadok.'" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/44.htm)
- **Constable**: "In every age the sovereign and gracious God has a remnant of those who cleave to Him" (Feinberg, cited). Allen suggested God gave this revelation "to settle disputes about the staffing of the post-exilic temple." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Bible.org**: "Here is a list of what the faithful Zadokian priests can and cannot do." (https://bible.org/book/export/html/21739)

---

### v. 17–19: Linen Garments; No Sweat; Changing Clothes

**Traditional Reading:**

The Zadokite priests must wear only linen garments when ministering in the inner court and temple — linen turbans and linen undergarments. No wool is permitted. They must not wear "anything that makes them perspire." When they go out to the outer court where the people are, they must take off the holy garments, leave them in the holy chambers, and put on other clothes, "so that they do not transmit holiness to the people with their garments."

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Linen symbolises "their calling to serve in God's peace and rest rather than in human sweat and effort." Wool, being an animal product, was associated with the curse of sweat (Gen 3:19). "God wanted His priests … to serve Him in the peace and rest of the Spirit, not the sweat of human effort apart from God." Trapp (cited) warns against the superstition that priestly vestments themselves sanctify: "The monks at this day make the silly people believe that they cannot be damned … if they be buried in a Franciscan's cowl." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **Constable**: "No fabric that caused them to sweat would be acceptable because perspiration would make them wet, and dry skin stays cleaner than sweaty skin. Wool may have been an unacceptable material too because it is a product of animals, whereas linen comes from plants" (Wevers, cited). When they changed clothes, they avoided transmitting holiness to the common realm (cf. Exod 29:37; 30:29; Lev 6:27; Hag 2:12). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Peake's (Critical)**: Notes that the sanctity of the dress "would have been transferred to the people with whom they came in contact, and rendered them unfit for secular occupations." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Benson**: The phrase "shall not gird themselves with any thing that causeth sweat" means "not with a woollen girdle, which may make them sweat during their laborious service about the altar, and make their garments smell offensively." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-44.html)

---

### v. 20–22: Hair, Wine, and Marriage Rules

**Traditional Reading:**

Priests must not shave their heads or let hair grow long, but trim it carefully. No priest may drink wine before entering the inner court. They must not marry a widow or divorced woman, but only a virgin of Israelite descent or the widow of another priest.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: On hair: "They were to avoid extremes in either way." Block (cited): "Like scarred skin, both the shaved head and long, unkempt hair were considered signs of disfigurement (cf. Lev 19:27)." On wine: "They must be in full control of their faculties so as to offer intelligent worship to God" (Wright, cited). The tragedy of Nadab and Abihu (Lev 10:9) illustrates the danger. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **Constable**: Long hair signified mourning; pagan idolatrous priests shaved all hair as a sign of mourning. Under the Mosaic system, the marriage restrictions bound only the high priest (Lev 21:7, 14), but "under the millennial system they will apply to all Zadokite priests." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Benson**: The hair prohibition was probably to distinguish Jewish priests from heathen priests, especially "the Egyptian priests of Isis and Serapis, who had their heads shaved and uncovered." The marriage restriction in the Mosaic law applied only to the high priest (Lev 21:13–14); "here it is applied to all the priests in general." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-44.html)

---

### v. 23–24: Teaching and Judging

**Traditional Reading:**

The priests are to "teach My people the difference between the holy and the common, and show them how to discern between the clean and the unclean." In disputes they are to officiate as judges according to God's ordinances. They must keep God's laws and statutes regarding all appointed feasts and Sabbaths.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: This conflates Leviticus 10:10–11, which highlights the priest's duty to distinguish and then to teach (*hora*) Israel. The judicial role "has a long history" — Deut 33:10 perceives it "as a natural corollary to the Levites' teaching responsibilities" (Block, cited). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **Constable**: "The priests were by their lives to be examples of separateness; their ritual holiness was intended to promote ethical holiness" (Taylor, cited). "This is also the duty of believer priests today (1 Pet 1:13–16)." Sabbath observance, though not part of New Covenant law, "God will reinstitute it during the kingdom dispensation." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Benson**: "Ministers should take pains to cause people to discern between the clean and the unclean, that they may not confound the distinctions between right and wrong." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-44.html)

---

### v. 25–27: Defilement by the Dead

**Traditional Reading:**

A priest must not defile himself by going near a dead person, except for immediate family: father, mother, son, daughter, brother, or unmarried sister. (The wife is excluded, as is a married daughter.) After cleansing, he counts seven days. On the day he re-enters the inner court to minister, he must present his sin offering.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Theirs will be a ministry of life, not death." The presence of death during the Millennium is noted: "There would be individuals entering the Millennium with natural bodies from the tribulation period … though physical life would be much longer" (Alexander, cited). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **Ellicott**: These instructions are "an exact repetition of Leviticus 21:1–4; but … there is added to the ordinary cleansing of seven days (Num 19:11–17) another period of seven days, after which Ezekiel requires (v. 27) the priest to offer a sin offering before entering again on his duties." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/44.htm)
- **Peake's (Critical)**: The exclusion of the wife "as she is not a blood-relation, and the married daughter, as, by her marriage, she has passed into another family." The uncleanness involved in contact with the dead probably contains "an implicit protest against the worship of the dead." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Constable**: "People will die during the Millennium (cf. Isa 65:20), but no one will die in the eternal state (Rev 21:4)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)

---

### v. 28–31: The Priests' Inheritance and Provision

**Traditional Reading:**

God Himself is the priests' inheritance; they receive no landed possession in Israel. They eat the grain offerings, sin offerings, and guilt offerings. Everything in Israel "devoted" (*herem*) to the LORD belongs to them. The best of all firstfruits and contributions — including the "first batch of dough" — goes to the priests, so that a blessing may rest on the giver's home. Priests may not eat any bird or animal found dead or torn by wild beasts.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Verses 28–29 are "a simple repetition of the frequent declarations in the law (Num 18:20; Deut 10:9; 18:2)." The first of the dough was given "so that a blessing may rest upon your homes." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-44/)
- **Peake's (Critical)**: "Formerly the sin-offering and the guilt-offering had been paid to them in money (2 Kgs 12:16)." The restriction in v. 31 "had formerly applied to all the people (Exod 22:31)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Benson**: "It is all in all to the comfort of any house to have the blessing of God upon it … the way to have the blessing of God upon our estates is, to honour God with them, and to give him and his ministers, him and his poor, their share out of them." He cites Prov 3:33 and notes the precept in Mal 3:8–12. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Constable**: The priests would receive "no other inheritance in the land but the privilege of serving the Lord." The devoted (*herem*) things were those "that the offerer could not redeem (buy back; cf. Lev 27:21, 28; Num 18:14)." Priests were not to eat animals that died naturally or were killed by beasts — these "might be inferior and might carry communicable diseases." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-44.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: The offering of firstfruits was "to provide for the physical needs of him and his family, in order that spiritual blessings might, through him, come upon the homes of all to whom they ministered" (Num 15:20; Prov 3:9–10; 1 Cor 9:9–14). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-44.html)

---

## Summary of Points Where Traditions Differ

1. **The identity of "the prince" (v. 3)**:
   - **Reformed (Ligonier, JFB's spiritual sense) and older Jewish interpreters**: Tends to see the prince as Messiah / Christ, with JFB explaining the prince as a civil ruler who "represents Messiah." Gill says outright "the King Messiah."
   - **Dispensationalist / Premillennial (Guzik, Constable, Gray's)**: The prince cannot be Christ because he offers a sin offering for himself and has sons. He is a future Davidic king (possibly resurrected David) who serves as Messiah's representative.
   - **Post-exilic / historicist (Benson, Methodist)**: Sees the prince as Zerubbabel or a post-exilic governor.

2. **The east gate and Mary (v. 1–2)**: Catholic and some older Protestant writers (noted by both Gill and Clarke) read the shut gate typologically as the perpetual virginity of Mary. Most modern Protestants do not adopt this reading.

3. **Priests vs. Levites distinction (vv. 10–16)**: Modern critical scholarship (Peake's) sees this passage as a pivotal moment in the *historical development* of the Israelite priesthood — Ezekiel innovates by creating a sharp priest/Levite distinction that influenced the Priestly (P) source of the Pentateuch. Traditional commentators read it as divine regulation, not human innovation.

4. **Millennium vs. eternal state**: Dispensationalist commentators (Constable, Guzik) see the presence of death (vv. 25–27), sin offerings, marriage, and childbirth as evidence that this temple belongs to a millennial (not eternal) phase. Covenant/amillennial readers may see the vision as symbolic of ideal worship or the church age.

5. **Application to church practice (vv. 6–9, 15–16)**: Gill and Guzik both draw direct applications to church membership and ministerial qualifications — unregenerate persons should not be admitted to church membership or ordained ministry. Constable applies the priests' teaching role to "believer priests today (1 Pet 1:13–16)."
